Before the chapter is over, a jar of manna is set aside to be kept for future generations.
17:
The Israelites move on from the Desert of Sin and camp at ⟦l:rephidim_996|Rephidim⟧, on the way to ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧. Once again there is no water, and this time the complaints turn dangerous. The people quarrel with ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, and he tells the Lord they are almost ready to stone him.

God sends ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ ahead with some of the elders to the rock at ⟦l:horeb_576|Horeb⟧, carrying the same staff that struck the ⟦l:nile_895|Nile⟧. When Moses strikes the rock, water comes out. He names the place ⟦l:massah_771|Massah⟧ and ⟦l:meribah_783|Meribah⟧, meaning testing and quarrelling, because the people asked, is the Lord among us or not? Israel's later psalms, and the New Testament after them, would recall those names as a warning.

Next, Israel fights its first battle. The Amalekites, a desert people descended from ⟦p:esau_1216|Esau⟧, attack the Israelites at ⟦l:rephidim_996|Rephidim⟧. Here we meet ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ for the first time, chosen by ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ to lead the fighting men. Moses climbs a hill with the staff of God, together with ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and a man named ⟦p:hur_1571|Hur⟧, and the outcome of the battle below follows the raising and lowering of Moses' hands. The conflict with ⟦l:amalek_53|Amalek⟧ will run on for generations.
18:
The story now turns to a visit at the ⟦l:mount_sinai_855|mountain of God⟧, where ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ first saw the burning bush and where the Israelites are camped. Word has reached ⟦l:midian_796|Midian⟧ of everything that has happened, and ⟦p:jethro_2431|Jethro⟧, Moses' father-in-law, comes out to meet him. With him are Moses' wife ⟦p:zipporah_3095|Zipporah⟧ and their two sons, ⟦p:gershom_1302|Gershom⟧ and ⟦p:eliezer_1114|Eliezer⟧. We learn here that Moses had sent them back to Jethro earlier.

It is a warm meeting. ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ bows to his father-in-law, kisses him, and tells him all that the Lord has done for Israel. ⟦p:jethro_2431|Jethro⟧, a priest of ⟦l:midian_796|Midian⟧ and not an Israelite, responds with praise and a confession: now I know that the Lord is greater than all other gods. He offers sacrifices, and ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and the elders of Israel share a meal with him in the presence of God.

The next day ⟦p:jethro_2431|Jethro⟧ watches ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ at work, sitting from morning until evening while the people bring him their disputes, and he sees at once that it cannot go on. His advice is practical and wise, and Moses takes it. The chapter shows a nation beginning to be organised, just before it receives the law that will govern it.
19:
Three months after leaving ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, the Israelites arrive in the Wilderness of ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧ and camp in front of the mountain. They will be here for almost a year. Everything from this chapter to the end of Exodus, all of Leviticus and the first part of Numbers takes place in this one location.

God had promised ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ at the burning bush that the people would worship him on this mountain, and now it has happened. Moses climbs up to meet God, and comes down with a message that sums up what God intends. You have seen what I did to ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, and how I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself. If you obey me and keep my covenant, you will be my treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The people answer together, we will do everything the Lord has said.

The rest of the chapter is preparation for the moment when God himself will come down on the mountain. The people must wash their clothes and consecrate themselves for three days, and a boundary is set around the base that no one may cross. On the morning of the third day the mountain is wrapped in smoke and fire, thunder and lightning break out, the ground shakes, and the sound of a ram's horn grows louder and louder.
20:
The mountain is covered in smoke and fire, and the people stand trembling at its foot. Now God speaks to them directly. These are the words known as the Ten Commandments, though Exodus here simply calls them all these words.

They begin not with a command but with a reminder of who is speaking: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, out of the house of slavery. Everything that follows rests on that rescue. The first commands concern Israel's relationship with God: no other gods, no idols, no misuse of his name, and the keeping of the Sabbath. The rest concern life among their neighbours: honour for parents, and protection for life, marriage, property, truth, and even the desires of the heart.

When the voice falls silent, the people are terrified. They beg ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ to speak to them himself, for fear that if God speaks again they will die. So they stand at a distance while Moses approaches the thick darkness where God is. Then come the first of the laws given to Moses there, about how Israel is to worship: with no images of gold or silver, and on a simple altar of earth or uncut stone.
21:
⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ has gone into the thick darkness on the mountain, and God continues to speak to him. What follows, running through to the end of chapter twenty-three, is a collection of laws that later in the book is called the Book of the Covenant. If the Ten Commandments are the foundation, these laws carry them into the fields, homes and quarrels of a farming people.

The laws open with the treatment of servants, and with limits on how long a Hebrew may be held in service. For a people just freed from slavery, that is where justice begins. Then come laws dealing with violence: murder and manslaughter, with places of refuge for those who kill by accident, injuries in a fight, and the principle of an eye for an eye, which in its setting set a limit on revenge and required that a penalty fit the harm done.

The chapter closes in the farmyard and the open country, among oxen and pits and neighbours. An ox that gores a man to death must be stoned, and if its owner was warned and did nothing, he answers with his own life. Other nations kept written laws, the code of the Babylonian king Hammurabi the best known among them, but these come from the mountain, from the God who has just set his people free.
22:
The laws given to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ on the mountain continue. This chapter begins with property, and with the principle of restitution. A thief must repay what he has taken, often several times over. There are rulings about a burglar caught at night, livestock that strays into a neighbour's field, a fire that spreads, and goods or animals left in someone else's care and then lost.

Then the subjects change more quickly, and the tone shifts. The laws move from compensation to holiness, and from the courtroom to the heart of God. Sorcery, bestiality and sacrifice to other gods are forbidden. Then come some of the most striking words in the collection. Israel must not oppress the foreigner, because they themselves were foreigners in ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧. They must not mistreat the widow or the orphan, because God hears their cry. They must not charge interest to the poor, and a cloak taken as security must be returned by sunset, because it may be the only covering a poor man has at night.

Last come the offerings that belong to God, including the firstborn, and a reminder of the reason behind all of it: you are to be my holy people.
23:
This is the last part of the Book of the Covenant. It begins with justice in the courts: no false reports, no siding with the crowd, no bribes, and fairness for rich and poor alike. Even an enemy's stray animal must be returned. Once again comes the reminder that Israel knows what it is to be a foreigner.

The laws then turn to the rhythms of time. Every seventh year the fields are to rest, so the poor and the wild animals can eat what grows. Every seventh day people and animals rest. Three times a year the men of Israel are to come before the Lord for the great festivals: Unleavened Bread in the spring, the Feast of Harvest when the first grain is gathered, and the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the agricultural year. The second is also called the Feast of Weeks, later known as Pentecost, and the third the Feast of Tabernacles.

Finally the Lord looks ahead to ⟦l:canaan_272|Canaan⟧. God promises to send his angel before Israel to guard them and bring them into the land, and he will drive out its inhabitants little by little. Israel must make no covenant with those nations or their gods, because their gods would become a snare.
24:
The Book of the Covenant is finished, and now the covenant is formally sealed. ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ comes down from the mountain and tells the people all the words and laws of the Lord, and they answer with one voice that they will do it all.

The ceremony that follows is one of the most important in the Old Testament. ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ writes down God's words, builds an altar at the foot of the mountain and sets up twelve pillars, one for each tribe. Young men offer sacrifices. Moses reads the Book of the Covenant aloud, the people promise again to obey, and he splashes blood on the altar and on the people, calling it the blood of the covenant. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ would use the same phrase centuries later, at the Last Supper.

Then ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ climbs the mountain with ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧, Aaron's sons ⟦p:nadab_2128|Nadab⟧ and ⟦p:abihu_33|Abihu⟧, and seventy elders of Israel. There they see the God of Israel, with something like a pavement of sapphire under his feet, and they eat and drink in his presence. Finally God calls Moses higher still, to receive tablets of stone. Taking ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ as his attendant, he leaves Aaron and ⟦p:hur_1571|Hur⟧ in charge below. For six days the cloud covers the mountain, and on the seventh the Lord calls to Moses, and he disappears into the cloud. He will be gone for forty days and forty nights.
25:
⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ is on the summit of ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧, inside the cloud, where he will stay for forty days. The covenant has been sealed, and now God tells him what comes next. The next seven chapters are God's instructions for a sanctuary, and the reason is given at the start: they are to make a sanctuary for me, so that I may dwell among them.

The materials are to come as a free offering from anyone whose heart moves them: gold, silver and bronze, fine yarns dyed blue, purple and scarlet, linen, goat hair, skins, acacia wood, oil, spices and precious stones. Many of these riches were carried out of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧. Everything is to be made according to the pattern God shows ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ on the mountain.

The instructions begin at the centre and work outward. First comes the ark, a chest of acacia wood covered in gold, which will hold the tablets of the covenant. Its lid, called the mercy seat, has two golden cherubim facing one another with outstretched wings, and God says he will meet ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ there. Then come the golden table for the Bread of the Presence and the lampstand, hammered from a single piece of gold, with seven lamps on branches shaped like an almond tree in blossom.
26:
The instructions for the sanctuary continue. Having described the ark, the table and the lampstand, God now describes the structure that will house them: the tabernacle itself, a tent designed to be taken down, carried and set up again wherever Israel travels.

Its innermost layer is a set of ten linen curtains in blue, purple and scarlet, with cherubim woven into them. Over these go curtains of goat hair, then coverings of ram skins dyed red and of fine leather. The tent stands on a framework of upright frames made of acacia wood and overlaid with gold, set in silver bases and held together with crossbars.

The most important detail comes near the end. Inside the tent a veil, embroidered with cherubim, divides the space into two rooms. Behind it, in the ⟦l:most_holy_place_826|Most Holy Place⟧, stands the ark with its mercy seat. In front of it, in the ⟦l:holy_place_574|Holy Place⟧, are the table and the lampstand. A further curtain closes the entrance. Every measurement is given in cubits, a cubit being about the length of a forearm, roughly half a metre.
27:
The tent and its furniture have been described. Now the instructions move outside, into the open air.

In front of the tent is to stand the great altar for burnt offerings, a hollow box of acacia wood covered in bronze, with a horn at each corner. It is about two and a half metres square, and every sacrifice in Israel's worship will be offered here. Around both the altar and the tent there is to be a courtyard, enclosed by linen curtains hung from posts, with an embroidered gate on the east side, toward the sunrise. Inside the tent, gold is the main metal, while out here in the courtyard bronze is used, and the materials grow plainer as one moves away from the presence of God.

The chapter ends with a brief command that leads into the next subject. The Israelites are to bring pure olive oil to keep the lamps burning, and ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and his sons are to tend them from evening until morning before the Lord. For the first time in these instructions the priests are mentioned, and they will be the subject of the next two chapters.
28:
God has described the tabernacle, its furniture and its courtyard. Now he turns to the people who will serve there. ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and his four sons, ⟦p:nadab_2128|Nadab⟧, ⟦p:abihu_33|Abihu⟧, ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧ and ⟦p:ithamar_649|Ithamar⟧, are to be set apart as priests, and this chapter describes their clothing, made by skilled craftsmen, for glory and for beauty.

⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧, as the high priest, is to wear a set of garments unlike anyone else's. Over a blue robe goes the ephod, a richly woven garment rather like an apron or vest, with two onyx stones on its shoulders, each engraved with the names of six of the tribes of Israel. On his chest he wears the breastpiece of judgment, set with twelve precious stones, each engraved with the name of a tribe. Inside it are the Urim and Thummim, objects used to seek God's will. So whenever Aaron enters the sanctuary he carries the names of Israel on his shoulders and over his heart.

Golden bells hang from the hem of his robe. On his turban he wears a gold plate engraved with the words: holy to the Lord. ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s sons are given simpler garments of their own.
29:
The priestly garments have been described. Now God gives instructions for the ceremony that will make ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and his sons priests. It is to last seven days, and it will be carried out, almost exactly as described here, in Leviticus chapter eight.

The ordination begins with washing at the entrance to the tent. ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ is dressed in his garments and anointed with oil poured on his head, and his sons are dressed too. Then three animals are sacrificed. A bull is offered as a sin offering, to deal with the priests' own sin; one ram is burned whole as a burnt offering; and the second ram, called the ram of ordination, provides blood that is put on the right ear, the right thumb and the big toe of the right foot of each new priest. Parts of this ram, with bread, are placed in the priests' hands and then burned, and they eat the rest at the tent's entrance.

The chapter then describes the daily offerings to be made on the altar, a lamb each morning and another at twilight, for all generations. And it ends with God's purpose for the whole tabernacle. There I will meet with Israel. I will dwell among them and be their God, the God who brought them out of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ so that he might dwell among them.
30:
The great instructions for the tabernacle are nearly complete, and this chapter adds a series of final items. The first is a small golden altar for incense, which is to stand in the ⟦l:holy_place_574|Holy Place⟧, just in front of the veil that hides the ark. ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ is to burn fragrant incense on it every morning and every evening, so that its smoke rises continually before the Lord.

Then comes a ruling for whenever a census is taken. Every man counted must pay half a shekel of silver, rich and poor alike, as a ransom for his life, and the money is to be used for the service of the tent. A bronze basin is to stand between the tent and the altar, so that the priests can wash their hands and feet before they serve.

The chapter closes with recipes for two sacred blends. One is the anointing oil, made with myrrh, cinnamon, fragrant cane, cassia and olive oil, to be used only for anointing the tabernacle, its furnishings and the priests. The other is the incense, made of spices and frankincense. Neither may be copied for ordinary use. They are holy.
31:
Forty days of instructions on the mountain are drawing to a close. God has described what is to be made; now he names who will make it. ⟦p:bezaleel_490|Bezalel⟧, from the tribe of Judah, the grandson of ⟦p:hur_1571|Hur⟧, is said to be filled with the ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|Spirit of God⟧, and here that gift brings skill in every kind of craft: metalwork, gem cutting, woodwork and design. ⟦p:aholiab_170|Oholiab⟧, from the tribe of ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧, is appointed to help him, along with other skilled craftsmen.

Then God gives ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ a final word about the Sabbath. Israel must keep it as a sign between God and his people for ever, and the penalty for breaking it is death. Six days they may work, but the seventh is a day of complete rest, because in six days the Lord made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh he rested.

Finally, when God has finished speaking with ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ on ⟦l:mount_sinai_855|Mount Sinai⟧, he gives him the two tablets of the covenant, tablets of stone written by the finger of God. Moses is about to carry them down the mountain. But while he has been receiving them, something has been happening in the camp below.
32:
While ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ has been on the mountain receiving the plans for God's dwelling, the people in the camp below have grown restless. Weeks have gone by with no sign of him. They gather around ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧, whom Moses left in charge, and demand gods to go before them. As for this Moses who brought us out of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, they say, we do not know what has happened to him.

⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ gives way. He collects their gold earrings and makes a calf, and the people declare that these are the gods who brought them out of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧. Aaron builds an altar and proclaims a feast to the Lord, and the next day becomes a riot of eating, drinking and revelry. The bull or calf was a common religious image in the ancient world, a symbol of strength and fertility. The people have broken the commandments they heard spoken from the mountain only weeks before.

On the summit, God tells ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ what has happened, and says he will destroy the people and make a great nation from Moses instead. What follows is one of the great intercessions of the Bible, as Moses pleads for Israel. Then he goes down the mountain, carrying the tablets, and comes within sight of the camp.
33:
The calf has been destroyed and the guilty punished, but the covenant is badly damaged. God tells ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ to lead the people on to the promised land, and he will send an angel ahead of them to drive out its inhabitants. But he himself will not go with them. They are a stiff-necked people, and if he went among them he might destroy them on the way. When the people hear this, they mourn and take off their jewellery.

The chapter then describes something ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ used to do. He would pitch a tent outside the camp, called the Tent of Meeting. This is not yet the tabernacle, which has still to be built, but a simpler tent where the pillar of cloud would come down, and where the Lord would speak with Moses face to face, as a man speaks with his friend. ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧, Moses' young assistant, would stay there.

What follows is among the most intimate conversations in the Old Testament. ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ refuses to go on without the presence of God. If your presence does not go with us, he says, do not send us up from here. And then he makes a bolder request still: please show me your glory.
34:
God has agreed to go with his people, and he has promised ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ a glimpse of his glory. Now Moses is told to cut two new stone tablets, like the ones he broke, and to climb ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧ again alone at first light.

What happens on the mountain is one of the high points of the Old Testament. The Lord descends in the cloud, passes in front of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and proclaims his own name: the Lord, the Lord God, compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness, forgiving iniquity, yet by no means leaving the guilty unpunished. These words, spoken just after the golden calf, became Israel's most treasured description of God, and they echo through the psalms and the prophets.

⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ bows to the ground and asks again that God would go with them and forgive. God renews the covenant, repeating some of its central commands, especially against making treaties with the peoples of ⟦p:canaan_914|Canaan⟧ or worshipping their gods. Moses stays on the mountain another forty days and nights. When he comes down with the new tablets, he does not know that his face is shining from speaking with the Lord.
35:
⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ has come down from the mountain with the new tablets, his face shining, and the covenant has been renewed. Now, at last, the work can begin. The final six chapters of Exodus describe the building of the tabernacle, and to a large extent they repeat, almost word for word, the instructions given earlier. The repetition carries its own message: everything God commanded is now done, exactly as he commanded it.

⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ gathers the whole community and begins with the Sabbath: six days for work, the seventh a holy day of rest, with no fire lit in their homes. Then he calls for the offering. Only a few chapters ago the people stripped off their gold to make a calf. Now men and women come with willing hearts, bringing brooches, earrings, rings and necklaces, fine yarn and linen, skins, wood, oil and spices. The leaders bring the precious stones for the high priest's garments, and the skilled women spin yarn and goat hair with their own hands.

Finally ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ presents the master craftsmen to the people. ⟦p:bezaleel_490|Bezalel⟧ of the tribe of Judah and ⟦p:aholiab_170|Oholiab⟧ of the tribe of ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧, filled with skill by God, will lead the work, and they are given the ability to teach others.
36:
The offerings have been brought, and the craftsmen are ready. ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ hands over to ⟦p:bezaleel_490|Bezalel⟧, ⟦p:aholiab_170|Oholiab⟧ and the other skilled workers everything the people have given. But the gifts keep coming, morning after morning, until the craftsmen come to Moses with an unusual problem: the people are bringing far more than is needed. Moses sends word through the camp, and the people are told to stop giving.

Then the building begins, and it begins, as the instructions did not, with the tent itself. The narrator describes the craftsmen making the ten linen curtains with their cherubim, joined by loops and golden clasps, then the curtains of goat hair for the tent over it, and the coverings of skins. After that come the gold-covered frames of acacia wood, standing on silver bases and held together with crossbars, then the embroidered veil and the curtain for the entrance.

Listeners who have heard chapter twenty-six will recognise every detail. Only the voice has changed. On the mountain God said, you shall make. Now, in the camp, the craftsmen make.
37:
The structure of the tabernacle has been made. Now ⟦p:bezaleel_490|Bezalel⟧ himself turns to the furniture for its two rooms, beginning with the most sacred object of all.

First comes the ark of acacia wood, overlaid with gold, with its poles for carrying and its golden lid, the mercy seat, with two cherubim of hammered gold facing one another, their wings spread over it. Then he makes the table for the Bread of the Presence, with its plates, dishes, bowls and pitchers of pure gold, and the lampstand, hammered from a single talent of gold, with its seven lamps and almond-blossom cups.

Last in the chapter is the small golden altar of incense, which is to stand before the veil, together with the sacred anointing oil and the fragrant incense. These were the last items described in the instructions on the mountain, and with them the furnishings of the inner tent are complete.
38:
The golden furnishings of the tent are finished. Now the work moves outside, to the bronze altar for burnt offerings and the bronze basin for washing. The basin, we are told, was made from the bronze mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, a detail the instructions did not include. Then comes the courtyard, with its linen curtains, its posts banded with silver and its embroidered gate.

The second half of the chapter is an inventory, an account of the materials, kept by the Levites under the direction of ⟦p:ithamar_649|Ithamar⟧, ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s son. ⟦p:bezaleel_490|Bezalel⟧ and ⟦p:aholiab_170|Oholiab⟧ are named once more as the master craftsmen. The quantities are large. About a tonne of gold was given, several tonnes of silver and bronze, and the silver came from the half shekel paid by every man counted in a census, a total of six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty men. The silver was cast into bases for the frames and posts of the sanctuary, and the bronze into the altar, the courtyard bases and the tent pegs.
39:
The tabernacle and its furnishings have been made. The last task is the clothing for the priests, and this chapter follows the craftsmen as they weave and stitch the garments described back in chapter twenty-eight. There is the ephod, with gold beaten into thin sheets and cut into threads to weave through the coloured yarn, and the two onyx stones on its shoulders, and the breastpiece with its twelve stones engraved with the names of the tribes. There is the blue robe with its bells and pomegranates, the tunics, turbans and sashes, and the gold plate engraved with the words: holy to the Lord.

Listen for the refrain that runs through this chapter: just as the Lord had commanded ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧. It is repeated again and again, like a seal pressed onto each finished piece.

Then the whole work is brought to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, item by item, from the tent and its clasps to the priests' garments. He inspects everything and sees that it has all been done exactly as the Lord commanded. And Moses blesses them. As at the end of the creation account in Genesis, the work is complete, it is examined, and a blessing is spoken.
40:
All the pieces of the tabernacle have been made and inspected. Now God tells ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ to put it all together. The date he gives is significant: the first day of the first month, at the beginning of a new year, almost exactly a year after Israel left ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧.

The chapter describes ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ setting up the tent with his own hands. He lays the bases and raises the frames, spreads the coverings, places the tablets in the ark and the ark behind the veil, and arranges the table, the lampstand and the golden altar in the ⟦l:holy_place_574|Holy Place⟧. In the courtyard he sets up the altar of burnt offering and the basin, and hangs the curtain at the gate. Once more the refrain sounds at each step: just as the Lord had commanded him. And at last, the simple sentence: so Moses finished the work.

What happens next is the climax of the whole book. The story that began with Israel enslaved in ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, building cities for ⟦p:pharaoh_2331|Pharaoh⟧, ends in a very different place. The cloud that led them out of Egypt and settled on ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧ now comes down upon the tent they have built.
